title: The triple Nāciketa: crossing birth and death
theme: One who has piled the Nāciketa fire three times, joined with the three, doing the three works, crosses birth and death; knowing the god, he reaches lasting peace.

words.meaning: one who has piled the Nāciketa [fire] three times
words.context: Śaṅkara: «त्रिः कृत्वा नाचिकेतोऽग्निश्चितो येन सः त्रिणाचिकेतः»
Śaṅkara: mother, father and teacher; Madhva: the Vedas

words.meaning: the knowing one born of Brahman
words.context: Śaṅkara: born of Hiraṇyagarbha and all-knowing; Raṅgarāmānuja: the individual self

sandhi.type: visarga before t; visarga after i before a vowel
sandhi.rule: Visarga before t becomes s, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः); after i the visarga becomes r before a vowel.
Final m stays before a vowel.
a + i → e: P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः). The base file wrote निचाय्य मां; the correction restores निचाय्येमां (corrections.json).
Final m stays before a vowel.

samasa.meaning: one who has piled the Nāciketa fire three times; the n becomes ṇ after tri
the knower born of Brahman (Śaṅkara: of Hiraṇyagarbha)

morphology.note: The ṇ of -ṇāciketa is the cerebralisation of n after r in tri (as in a compound, P. 8.4.3 (पूर्वपदात्‌ संज्ञायामगः) and following); Madhva’s digital text writes the dental n (a witness error, corrections.json).
Absolutive of ni-cāy ‘observe, perceive’; Śaṅkara: ‘having seen as oneself’, Madhva’s commentators: ‘having considered’.

translation.literal: ‘One who has thrice [piled] the Nāciketa [fire], having come to union with the three, a doer of the three works, crosses birth and death. Having known the knower born of Brahman, the god to be praised, having perceived [him], he goes to this peace completely.’
translation.readable: ‘Whoever has built the Nāciketa fire three times, joined with the three and doing the three works, crosses beyond birth and death. Knowing the all-knowing god born of Brahman, the one to be praised, and seeing him, he reaches this peace for ever.’

syntax: Two sentences with the same subject. In the first, triṇāciketaḥ and trikarmakṛt describe the subject and tribhir etya sandhim the condition; the verb is tarati janmamṛtyū. In the second, two absolutives (viditvā, nicāyya) lead to the verb eti, with śāntim atyantam as its goal.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: mother, father and teacher, whose teaching one has rightly received: «त्रिभिः मातृपित्राचार्यैः एत्य प्राप्य सन्धिं सन्धानं सम्बन्धम्»; or the Veda, smṛti and the learned; or perception, inference and scripture: «वेदस्मृतिशिष्टैर्वा प्रत्यक्षानुमानागमैर्वा». Madhva: the Vedas — «त्रिभिरेत्य सन्धिं वेदैरविरुद्धः», not contrary to the Vedas. Raṅgarāmānuja: the three fires, through meditation on the Supreme.

Śaṅkara: sacrifice, study and giving, «त्रिकर्मकृत् इज्याध्ययनदानानां कर्ता». Madhva: sacrifice, giving and austerity, citing the Gītā: «त्रिकर्मकृत् यज्ञदानतपःकर्ता». Raṅgarāmānuja gives both Śaṅkara’s list and a second: the cooked offerings, oblations and soma rites.

Śaṅkara: born of Brahman (Hiraṇyagarbha) and all-knowing: «ब्रह्मणो हिरण्यगर्भाज्जातो ब्रह्मजः ब्रह्मजश्चासौ ज्ञश्चेति ब्रह्मजज्ञः». Raṅgarāmānuja, following the Śrībhāṣya: the individual self, born of Brahman and a knower, «ब्रह्मणो जातत्वात् ज्ञत्वाच्च». Madhva, citing the Nāmanirukta: Hari, manifest from the Veda and all-knowing (see the commentary).

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: Two lines of 22 syllables, regular (with the corrected निचाय्येमां).

beginner: Death now praises the fire he has taught. A person who builds this fire three times, who lives in harmony with the three — whom the commentators identify differently as parents and teacher, the Vedas, or the sacred fires — and who performs the three duties of sacrifice, giving and either study or austerity, goes beyond birth and death. Then, knowing the shining one born of Brahman and seeing him, he reaches a lasting peace. The verse links ritual with knowledge: the fire alone is not the end, it is joined to understanding. The commentators argue at length about who the three are and who the god is.
analogy: Like a long climb in three stages, where the last stage is not a further step but a view that opens once you arrive.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: One who piles the fire three times, joined with the three and doing the three works, crosses birth and death; knowing and seeing the god born of Brahman, he reaches lasting peace.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Still as praise of action: «पुनरपि कर्मस्तुतिमेवाह». The fruit is reaching the state of Virāj by combining knowledge and ritual: «वैराजं पदं ज्ञानकर्मसमुच्चयानुष्ठानेन प्राप्नोतीत्यर्थः». The ‘peace’ is the cessation known within: «इमां स्वबुद्धिप्रत्यक्षां शान्तिम् उपरतिम्».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The triṇāciketa is one who studies the three anuvākas of the Nāciketa (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.11.7): «इत्याद्यनुवाकत्रयाध्यायी». The union is meditation on the Supreme; perceiving means seeing oneself as having Brahman for one’s self: «ब्रह्मात्मकं स्वात्मानं साक्षात्कृत्य». He cites the Śrībhāṣya’s gloss on brahmajajña: «जीवात्मानम् उपासकं ब्रह्मात्मकत्वेनावगम्य इत्यर्थः».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Madhva’s own lines: ‘with the three’ means not contrary to the Vedas, «वेदैरविरुद्धः», knowing the Lord as the Veda teaches, «वेदोक्तप्रकारेण भगवत्तत्वादिकं जानन्नित्यर्थः»; the three works are sacrifice, giving and austerity, «त्रिकर्मकृत् यज्ञदानतपःकर्ता», as the Gītā says: «यज्ञदानतपःकर्म न त्याज्यं कार्यमेव तत्». In his comment filed at 1.1.18 he cites the Nāmanirukta for brahmajajña: the Veda is ‘brahman’, Hari is manifest from it, and he is the knower: «ब्रह्मजस्तेन कथितस्स एव ज्ञोऽखिलज्ञतः».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The base file read निचाय्य मां, ‘having perceived me’; the other three witnesses and Śaṅkara’s gloss («निचाय्य दृष्ट्वा चात्मभावेन इमां स्वबुद्धिप्रत्यक्षां शान्तिम्») have निचाय्येमां, ‘having perceived, this [peace]’, and the edition corrects to it (corrections.json).

advaita.text: Praise of ritual combined with knowledge, whose fruit is the state of Virāj, not release: «वैराजं पदं ज्ञानकर्मसमुच्चयानुष्ठानेन प्राप्नोतीत्यर्थः». brahmajajña is Hiraṇyagarbha’s offspring, the all-knowing.

visistadvaita.text: The verse teaches release through ritual joined to meditation on the Supreme; brahmajajña is the individual self, to be known as having Brahman for its self: «जीवात्मानम् उपासकं ब्रह्मात्मकत्वेनावगम्य इत्यर्थः».

dvaita.text: Ritual done in accord with the Vedas aids knowledge of the Lord; brahmajajña is Hari, «ब्रह्मजस्तेन कथितस्स एव ज्ञोऽखिलज्ञतः», and the fruit is not reached by knowing the fire alone: «न चाग्निपरिज्ञानमात्रेणानन्तलोकाप्तिर्भगवज्ज्ञानं विना».

schools.disagreement: The verse is a test case for the relation of ritual and knowledge. For Śaṅkara its fruit (crossing birth and death) is figurative — a long-lasting state, Virāj — because ritual cannot release. For Raṅgarāmānuja and Madhva it belongs to release, reached by ritual joined to knowledge of the Lord. They also identify brahmajajña three different ways: Hiraṇyagarbha’s offspring, the individual self, Hari.

parallels.note: Cited by Madhva for the ‘three works’: sacrifice, giving and austerity, which the Gītā says must not be abandoned.
Cited by Śaṅkara for ‘the three’: knowledge is reliable when received from mother, father and teacher, as the Bṛhadāraṇyaka says of one who teaches well.

contemporary.text: The verse joins repeated practice (the fire built three times, the three duties) with understanding (knowing and seeing). Many disciplines say the same: practice prepares, but the change comes when one understands what the practice was for. (A modern reflection.)

reflect.beginner: What do you do regularly that you have never stopped to understand?
reflect.deeper: Can doing the right things, by themselves, bring peace? What does the verse add to them?
reflect.practice: Choose one routine act today and, before doing it, say to yourself what it is for.

references.text: Śaṅkara cites the Bṛhadāraṇyaka for teaching from mother, father and teacher; Madhva the Gītā (18.5) and the Nāmanirukta; Raṅgarāmānuja the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (3.11.7) and the Śrībhāṣya on Brahmasūtra 1.2.12 and 1.4.6. These are reported as cited by them.

flags.note: निचाय्येमां restores the reading of GRETIL, the vishvAsa mūla, Madhva’s text and Śaṅkara’s gloss for the base file’s निचाय्य मां (corrections.json).
brahmajajña is read as Hiraṇyagarbha’s all-knowing offspring (Śaṅkara), the individual self (Raṅgarāmānuja, Śrībhāṣya) or Hari (Madhva, citing the Nāmanirukta).
